what_its_for: Pegloticase is used to treat chronic gout in adults when other gout medicines have not worked well enough. It works by breaking down uric acid in your blood. Uric acid is the substance that builds up and causes painful gout attacks, joint damage, and lumps called tophi under your skin.
how_to_take: Pegloticase is NOT a pill you take at home. It is given as an IV infusion (a slow drip into your vein) by a healthcare provider in a clinic, hospital, or doctor's office. Each infusion takes at least 2 hours. You will be given allergy medicines (like antihistamines and steroids) before every infusion to help prevent reactions. You must stay at the clinic for at least 1 hour after your infusion so staff can watch for any reactions. Never try to give this medicine to yourself at home.
dosing: The usual dose is 8 mg given by IV infusion once every 2 weeks. Your doctor will check your uric acid blood levels regularly. If your uric acid level stays too high (above 6 mg/dL) on two tests in a row, your doctor may stop treatment because the medicine may not be working well enough for you.
missed_dose: If you miss or need to reschedule your infusion appointment, call your doctor or clinic right away to set up a new appointment as soon as possible. Try not to skip doses, because missing infusions can make the medicine less effective and may increase your risk of having a gout flare or an allergic reaction at your next infusion.
storage: You will not store this medicine at home — it is stored and prepared by healthcare professionals. If you are ever given vials to transport, keep them refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C). Do not freeze it. Do not shake the vials. Keep them in the original carton to protect from light.
what_to_avoid: Do not start any new uric acid-lowering medicines (such as allopurinol or febuxostat) while you are receiving pegloticase, as they can hide whether the medicine is working. Tell your doctor about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take. Avoid skipping infusion appointments. If you have G6PD deficiency (a genetic blood disorder), you must NOT use this medicine — tell your doctor before starting treatment.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room immediately if you notice any of these during or after your infusion: chest pain or tightness, trouble breathing or shortness of breath, flushing, redness, or rash, dizziness or fainting, swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat, nausea or vomiting, or feeling very unwell. Also call your doctor if you notice signs of a gout flare (increased joint pain or swelling), signs of infection, skin sores or ulcers that are not healing, or any unusual symptoms between infusions.
when_it_works: Pegloticase starts lowering your uric acid levels quickly, often within the first few weeks of treatment. However, gout flares (painful attacks) may actually happen MORE often in the first few months as your body dissolves old uric acid crystals. This is normal and does not mean the medicine is not working. Your doctor may give you medicines to help prevent these flares. It may take several months of regular treatment before you notice your gout symptoms, tophi lumps, and joint pain truly improve.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: It is not known if pegloticase is safe during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Talk to your doctor before using this medicine if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. G6PD deficiency: This medicine should NOT be used if you have G6PD deficiency because it can cause a serious condition called hemolytic anemia (destruction of red blood cells). Heart failure: Use with caution — tell your doctor if you have heart problems, as infusion reactions may be harder to manage. Kidney or liver disease: Your doctor will monitor you closely. This medicine has not been well studied in children.
